node.label: Tandem
node.summary: An AI study planner that turns your syllabus and deadlines into a realistic weekly plan, then adapts when life happens.

node.label: Price-conscious free-tier trialists
node.summary: Students who will try new tools if there is a real free tier but balk at $8/month, compare against free tiers of Notion, Todoist, ChatGPT and MyStudyLife, and churn subscriptions regularly.

node.label: Time-starved outcome buyers
node.summary: Busy students who will pay readily if the tool demonstrably saves hours per week and cuts planning busywork.

node.label: Entrenched incumbent-tool users
node.summary: Long-time Notion/Todoist/MyStudyLife/ChatGPT users who already pay for a tool, demand painless import and export, and question whether an AI planner is just a wrapper.

node.label: Group-chat-driven adopters
node.summary: Students who adopt what their friends vouch for; switching stories from friends drive their decisions, mostly discovered via TikTok and word of mouth.

node.label: Privacy-first AI skeptics
node.summary: Students who have left tools over training on user content and require a clear privacy policy and proof the AI works before uploading coursework.

node.label: Privacy and data-training concerns
node.summary: Widespread refusal to upload study materials without a clear privacy policy; multiple users left incumbents over training on user content.

node.label: Subscription fatigue and $8 feeling steep
node.summary: Students resist another $8/month subscription, prefer one-time purchase, and benchmark against free tiers.

node.label: Heavy setup and learning curve
node.summary: Onboarding over five minutes is a dealbreaker; users spent weekends configuring Todoist/Notion/MyStudyLife and abandoned them.

node.label: Unreliable, gimmicky AI and crashes
node.summary: Tools that are confidently wrong or crash erode trust; the space is seen as full of demos that break on real use.

node.label: Switching cost: import/export and lock-in
node.summary: Users won't move without import from MyStudyLife/Todoist and fear being unable to export.

node.label: Weak mobile and offline support
node.summary: Most planning happens on phones; incumbent mobile apps are called unusable and offline use on commutes is needed.

node.label: Doubt it's more than a ChatGPT wrapper
node.summary: Some ask why not use ChatGPT, Notion or Todoist directly.

node.label: Desire to automate planning busywork and save hours
node.summary: Strong demand for automation that incumbents only half deliver; saving a few hours a week is an instant buy.

node.label: Desire for a simple, decent planner
node.summary: Anticipation for a well-built, simple study planner; many follow new launches closely.

node.label: Planner incumbents racing to add AI amid price rises
node.summary: Notion, Todoist, ChatGPT and MyStudyLife reported raising prices while startups add AI features.

node.label: Data-policy backlash against incumbents
node.summary: All four named competitors face backlash over data policy changes, raising privacy expectations.

node.label: Rise of indie study planner tools
node.summary: Indie tools gaining ground against incumbents.

node.label: Youth subscription fatigue
node.summary: Surveys and posts report fatigue with recurring app fees among younger buyers.

node.label: AI hype fatigue
node.summary: Users tired of 'AI-powered' labels and gimmick tools.

node.label: Notion
node.summary: Feature-rich with a free tier but brutal learning curve, weak mobile, recent price rise and data-policy backlash.

node.label: MyStudyLife
node.summary: Category incumbent with a free tier, criticised for crashes, inaccuracy, unusable mobile app and training on user content; users leaving.

node.label: ChatGPT
node.summary: Default free alternative; users stick with it above $8 but report inaccuracy, crashes, poor mobile and data-policy concerns.

node.label: Todoist
node.summary: Task manager with free tier that only half-automates study planning; setup heavy, recent price rise and data backlash.

node.label: Incumbent free tiers
node.summary: Free tiers of Notion, Todoist, ChatGPT and MyStudyLife are the main comparison anchor.

node.label: Under-$8 trial ceiling
node.summary: Many say they'd try only below $8/month; $8 is perceived as the ubiquitous subscription price.

node.label: Budget stated WTP
node.summary: Price-conscious and incumbent users state WTP around $4–6.

node.label: Value-driven WTP
node.summary: Time-savers and peer-led adopters state WTP of roughly $9–12.

node.label: New frontier AI model release raises expectations and capability
Apple native AI features may compete with or normalise AI planning

event.question: In your own words, what is this product and who is it for?
event.answer: Tandem is an AI study planner: you feed it your syllabus and deadlines and it builds a realistic weekly plan, then reshuffles it when things slip. It's for university students like me who'd rather spend time actually working than planning the work.

event.question: Walk me through how you decided what to do about it.
event.answer: I heard about it through friends, mainly Fin, and the time-saving pitch hooked me immediately. I sat in 'considering' for a while because my real question was how heavy the setup is, and I eventually signed up mostly on the strength of the promise and Fin's enthusiasm, though I still haven't fully validated the onboarding.

event.question: What bothers you about it, or would stop you from using it?
event.answer: My biggest worry is setup: if I have to manually enter every module, reading and deadline, I've lost the hours it's supposed to save me. I'm also wary about mobile and offline support, since I plan on my phone between labs and on trains, and a weak app would kill it for me.

event.question: What would you realistically pay, and why that number?
event.answer: Honestly $8 a month feels fair, even cheap, if it saves me an hour a week; I'd pay up to about $12. Past that I'd start comparing it against just prompting ChatGPT for a plan, which is free-ish.

event.question: Where would you expect to hear about something like this, and what message would convince you?
event.answer: Friends and Reddit threads, maybe TikTok study creators. What would convince me is a short demo showing someone uploading a syllabus PDF and getting a usable week plan in under five minutes, plus the plan auto-adjusting on mobile when they miss a session.

event.question: Would you recommend it to a friend? What exactly would you tell them?
event.answer: Yes, cautiously. I'd tell them it's worth trying if they hate planning, the price is reasonable for the time it saves, but check how long setup takes and whether the phone app works well for them before committing.

event.answer: Tandem is an AI study planner: you feed it your syllabus and deadlines and it builds a realistic weekly plan, then reshuffles it when your week falls apart. It's for university students, especially people like me juggling shifts and classes who don't have time to plan manually.

event.question: Walk me through how you decided what to do about it.
event.answer: I saw it on TikTok, someone showing their chaotic week getting rebuilt automatically after a missed day, and that hit home because my work schedule changes constantly. I figured if it saves me even an hour a week on planning, $8 is nothing, so I signed up and tried it on my actual syllabi instead of overthinking it.

event.question: What bothers you about it, or would stop you from using it?
event.answer: My big worry is whether the AI actually works or just spits out generic plans I end up fixing by hand, because then it's just Notion with extra steps.
